title: SDK cost and latency profiling playbook for local development
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

This playbook describes a lightweight, reproducible process for profiling SDK calls in a local development environment with the dual goals of: 1) estimating per-request token and compute cost, and 2) measuring end-to-end latency distributions. The intent is to give SDK authors, integrators, and support engineers a small, repeatable toolkit that produces comparable metrics across machines and CI so we can make better tradeoffs for batching, caching, and model selection.

When to use this playbook

- During SDK feature development that touches request/response size or streaming behavior.
- Before a public SDK release to validate that new default timeouts, retries or adapters do not add >10% latency regressions.
- When a customer reports increased token cost or slow responses for a specific integration.

Goals and success criteria

- Obtain a stable sample (n >= 100) of request latencies and token counts for representative scenarios.
- Surface outliers and tail latency (p95, p99).
- Calculate an estimated cost-per-call using our internal price sheet.
- Produce an actionable recommendation: e.g., enable prompt batching in client, decrease max_tokens default, or add local caching.

Owners and contacts

- Document owner: Maya Chen (developer experience)
- On-call SME for profiling: eng-devx-profiling rotation (Slack: #devx-profiling)
- Support escalation: customer-success/observability team

Quickstart: run a profiling session locally

Prerequisites

1) Python 3.10+ virtualenv with SDK branch checked out.
2) Access token in REDWOOD_API_KEY (or local runtime token for private deployments).
3) jq and curl installed for quick data transformation.

Step-by-step

1) Create a sample workload file (sample-workload.json) with 100 requests that reflect your integration patterns (mix of short prompts, long-context prompts, and streaming). See example below.
2) Run the harness: ./tools/local_profile_runner.py --workload sample-workload.json --output runs/2026-04-12.json --concurrency 8
3) Collect raw metrics: cat runs/2026-04-12.json | jq -r '.[] | [ .request_id, .duration_ms, .tokens_in, .tokens_out, .status ] | @csv' > runs/summary.csv

Commands (example)

# run the profile harness (docker-compose optional)
python3 tools/local_profile_runner.py \
  --workload sample-workload.json \
  --output runs/local-profile.json \
  --concurrency 4 \
  --retries 1

# basic latency summary
cat runs/local-profile.json | jq -s 'map(.duration_ms) | {count: length, mean: (add/length), p95: (.[(length*0.95)|floor]), p99: (.[(length*0.99)|floor])}'

Sample workload JSON (abbreviated)

{
  "requests": [
    { "id": "short-1", "prompt": "Summarize: AI is...", "temperature": 0.0, "max_tokens": 50 },
    { "id": "long-1", "prompt": "Customer transcript: [long text placeholder]", "temperature": 0.2, "max_tokens": 350 },
    { "id": "stream-1", "prompt": "Live update: ...", "stream": true }
  ]
}

What the harness records

- request_id: unique id for correlation
- start_ts / end_ts / duration_ms
- tokens_in (prompt tokens) and tokens_out (generated tokens) per the local tokenizer
- network_ms (time spent in client-to-host + host-to-service)
- server_processing_ms (if the host returns this header)
- response_size_bytes
- sdk_adapter (python/js/http2/grpc)
- error classification (timeout, http5xx, client_err)

Minimum profiling table and thresholds

| Metric | Target (local dev) | Action if exceeded |
|---|---:|---|
| mean latency (ms) | < 350 | Investigate client adapter and DNS/resolution; run with --concurrency 1 to isolate per-call latency |
| p95 latency (ms) | < 1000 | Trace long tail calls, capture server_processing_ms, consider increasing timeout or switching model variant |
| token estimation error (%) | < 5% | Verify tokenizer settings and prompt trimming |
| request error rate | < 1% | Confirm retries/backoff and inspect server-side error codes |

(Note: the table above is presented as text — use the internal docs table UI when publishing.)

Advanced measurements: wall-time vs server-time

- wall-time = client observed duration_ms. This includes local serialization, network, and server time.
- server_time is returned by the Redwood host (X-Server-Processing-Ms header). Not all deployments include this; for private deployments ask the deployment owner to enable the header.

If server_time is missing, derive a conservative estimate: server_processing_ms = duration_ms - network_ms - client_serialization_ms. Capture client_serialization_ms by running a loop against a local stub (see below).

Local stub for adapter-only profiling

Purpose: isolate SDK adapter latency (serialization + local middleware) from remote server time.

- Start a tiny stub server: python3 tools/local_stub.py --port 8088 --delay-ms 10 --return-tokens 32
- Point SDK base_url to http://localhost:8088 and run the same workload. The difference between real run and stub run approximates network+server time.

Telemetry assertions and golden trace

Goal: produce a small JSON assertion that CI can check against to prevent regressions. The assertion file (prof_assertions.json) contains keys for mean_latency_ms, p95_ms, token_rate, and max_error_rate. CI job will run the harness with a fixed seed and compare.

Example assertion (prof_assertions.json):

{
  "mean_latency_ms": 320,
  "p95_latency_ms": 820,
  "token_rate_per_second": 45,
  "max_error_rate_percent": 1.0
}

CI integration notes

- Add a lightweight CI pipeline that runs the harness with concurrency=2 and a trimmed workload of 30 requests. Keep it under 10 minutes and mark as non-blocking on flaky cloud networks.
- If assertions drift consistently, run a nightly profile job and create a regression issue rather than failing PRs.

Troubleshooting guide (common patterns)

1) Observed p95 spike but mean stable
   - Check for head-of-line blocking from large streaming responses. Re-run with streaming disabled.
   - Investigate retry storms: check sdk_adapter logs for overlapping retries.

2) Tokens_in discrepancy between local tokenizer and server
   - Ensure SDK tokenizer version matches runtime tokenizer (tokenizer versions are pinned in tools/tokenizers/versions.txt). Recompute tokens locally with that binary.

3) Intermittent 5xx errors during profiling
   - Confirm rate limits on the test account; use a dedicated sandbox key.
   - If errors persist, capture full request/response (with redaction) and post to #devx-profiling.

Recommendations and common mitigations

- Batching: For high-throughput integrations, measure token_rate_per_second vs latency tradeoff. Use client-side bundling when single-call latency sensitivity is low.
- Streaming: For interactive UX, prioritize p95 tail fixes (smaller chunk sizes, backpressure).
- Local caching: Cache embeddings and reuse prompt prefixes when appropriate.
- Default max_tokens: reduce default max_tokens in the SDK for generation helpers to avoid accidental runaway costs. Document this change in release notes.

Example metrics exporter (YAML) for local Prometheus pushgateway

# pushgateway_job.yaml
job_name: "local-sdk-profile"
static_configs:
  - targets: ['localhost:9091']
  labels:
    env: local

Use cases: attach the exporter to tests to publish the following metrics: sdk_request_duration_ms, sdk_tokens_in, sdk_tokens_out, sdk_error_count.

Runbook: escalate and create a canonical fix

1) Capture a minimal repro workload and run the harness with --verbosity debug.
2) If the issue is reproducible, create an issue in repo: devx/sdk-profiles with the run artifact attached and label with severity (minor/regression/customer-impact).
3) Triage meeting: include SDK owner, runtime SRE, and a support engineer. Run the golden trace comparison and decide whether to rollback, patch, or document a workaround.

Appendix: Helpful snippets

- Token counting (Python):

from tokenizers import Tokenizer
tok = Tokenizer.from_file('tools/tokenizers/byte_level.json')
def count_tokens(text):
    return len(tok.encode(text).ids)

- Minimal HTTP adapter trace header capture (curl):

curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate" -d '{"prompt":"x"}'

Hand-off checklist for SDK releases that touch defaults

- Run this profiling harness against the release candidate.
- Attach prof_assertions.json to the release PR.
- Update release notes with expected change in cost-per-call and recommended mitigation for integrators.

FAQ

Q: Can we use this to estimate production cost?
A: This playbook gives a reproducible estimate for development and early QA. For true production cost modeling, run the same workload against a Dedicated environment and consult the billing team for commit/discount math.

Q: My CI is flaky; should assertions be blocking?
A: No. Keep them advisory unless you can provide a very stable private infra baseline. Nightly regression alerts are preferred.
